title: Dream and Promise Act Gains Urgency as Courts Battle Over Immigrant Work Permits
excerpt: With federal judges blocking work authorization cuts for TPS holders and deportation fears mounting, a bipartisan bill offering a pathway to citizenship for millions of Dreamers sits stalled in Congress.
body:
• The American Dream and Promise Act of 2025, cosponsored by over 200 lawmakers, would create a pathway to citizenship for an estimated 3.4 million Dreamers and Temporary Protected Status holders.
  • A federal judge on July 22 blocked the Trump administration from stripping tens of thousands of TPS holders of their work permits, adding fuel to demands for a legislative fix.
  • DACA recipients contribute roughly $6.2 billion in federal taxes and $3.3 billion in state and local taxes annually, according to the Center for American Progress.

A Bipartisan Bill With No Path Forward

As courts and the Trump administration wage parallel battles over immigrant work authorizations, a bipartisan bill that could offer permanent relief to millions remains parked in committee with no vote in sight.

https://x.com/repdeliaramirez/status/2080305261558763966

The American Dream and Promise Act of 2025 (H.R. 1589), reintroduced in February by Rep. Sylvia Garcia (D-TX) and co-led by Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-FL), would grant conditional permanent residence and eventually citizenship to Dreamers — undocumented immigrants brought to the United States as children — as well as recipients of Temporary Protected Status and Deferred Enforced Departure. The bill has 201 cosponsors and endorsements from nearly 120 organizations, including the AFL-CIO, the ACLU, and the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

It has not advanced beyond the House Judiciary and Education and Workforce committees.

The Stakes Keep Rising

On July 22, U.S. District Judge Nathaniel Gorton in Boston temporarily blocked the administration from revoking work permits for tens of thousands of TPS holders from El Salvador, Sudan, and Ukraine, according to Reuters. The ruling found that new restrictions from the 2025 tax and spending law had been retroactively applied without proper public notice.

The same week, a separate court order extended protections for roughly 350,000 Haitian TPS holders until July 27, after the administration moved to terminate their status. A Senate effort to extend Haitian TPS until 2029 — legislation that had already passed the House — failed to reach the floor on July 22. The Supreme Court ruled in June that it lacked jurisdiction to review DHS decisions on TPS, leaving the door open for terminations covering more than a dozen countries.

"Our nation cannot afford to lose the small business owners, the talent, the artists, the aspiring public servants, and the drive that Dreamers bring. If that's not American, I don't know what is."

— Rep. Sylvia Garcia (D-TX), bill sponsor

The Economic Argument

The average DACA recipient arrived in the United States at age six and has lived here for two decades, according to FWD.us. Collectively, DACA recipients earned $27.9 billion in 2022 and contributed $2.1 billion to Social Security and Medicare — benefits they cannot access.

The Center for American Progress estimates that granting Dreamers a pathway to citizenship could boost national GDP by $799 billion over the next decade and create hundreds of thousands of jobs. Garcia warned in a floor speech that ending DACA in Texas alone would cause an estimated 2,600 job losses per month, including 200 healthcare positions and 100 educators.

The healthcare workforce is already strained by TPS terminations. In Florida, nursing homes and group care facilities face staffing crises as Haitian TPS holders — who make up a significant share of direct care workers — lose authorization.

Indian Diaspora Connection

The bill carries particular relevance for the Indian American community. A previous version that passed the House in 2021 included provisions preventing children of H-1B visa holders from "aging out" of the immigration system at 21 — a problem affecting thousands of Indian families stuck in decade-long green card backlogs. The legislation would freeze children's ages for green card eligibility, allowing them to remain in legal status while their families wait.

Indian American lawmakers have been vocal supporters. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA) cosponsored the 2025 bill. Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-WA), who came to the United States at 16, called for legislation to protect Dreamers "from cruel mass deportation campaigns."

"Dreamers shape every aspect of American life. They are our neighbors, classmates, nurses, police officers, teachers, community leaders. It's long overdue that we give them citizenship."

— Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA)

What Happens Next

The bill faces long odds. The Republican-controlled House has shown no appetite for a vote. Before his inauguration, President Trump indicated he wanted to work with Democrats on Dreamer protections, but no such effort has materialized. The administration has instead pursued debanking undocumented immigrants, ending TPS designations, and cutting legal representation for unaccompanied minors in immigration court.

Judge Gorton's temporary block on TPS work permit revocations expires pending an August 5 ruling. Haitian TPS holders have until July 27. With legislative relief unlikely, millions of immigrants face a legal landscape that shifts week by week — and a Congress that has yet to act.
